headline: Saudi third-party logistics heads for $4.94bn as shippers stop owning warehouses
deck: Outsourcing distribution is a decision about capital and volatility before it is a decision about cost.
excerpt: Third-party logistics warehousing in Saudi Arabia is put at around $3.74bn in 2026, forecast to reach $4.94bn by 2031. The growth comes from shippers concluding that owning a distribution network is a worse use of capital than renting one.
content:
Third-party logistics is one of the declared segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo, and it is the segment whose growth says most about how the Kingdom's supply chains are maturing.

The market is put at around $3.74bn in 2026, forecast to reach $4.94bn by 2031. Growth of that order is not primarily a story about logistics costs falling. It is a story about who owns the assets.

A manufacturer or retailer that runs its own distribution network holds warehouses, racking, handling equipment, a fleet and the people to operate all of it. That capital is committed against a demand forecast, and it is sized for the peak. In a business with seasonal or promotional volatility, the network spends much of the year underused, and the cost of that idle capacity sits on the shipper's balance sheet.

A third-party operator running the same activity for several clients can smooth that. Different customers peak at different times, a shared facility runs closer to capacity year-round, and the operator's investment in automation is justified by aggregate volume that no single client could support. The shipper converts a capital commitment into an operating cost that scales with what it actually ships.

That is the structural case, and it is why outsourcing tends to accelerate in markets at a particular stage: once volumes are large enough to interest a serious operator, and once the shipper's growth is fast enough that building its own capacity would consume capital it would rather put into product.

Saudi Arabia is at that stage in several categories at once. Retail and e-commerce volumes have grown into a scale that justifies dedicated fulfilment operations. Pharmaceutical distribution demands validated cold chain that most manufacturers would rather not build. Industrial spare parts and aftermarket distribution — the service layer behind the Kingdom's growing installed base of plants and equipment — is a classic third-party category because the inventory is broad, slow-moving and expensive to hold.

The counter-argument is control, and it is a real one. Outsourcing distribution means outsourcing the last physical contact a business has with its customer, and service failures are attributed to the brand rather than to the contractor. The contracts that work are the ones written against measurable service levels with the data to prove them, which is why warehouse management and telematics systems matter more in an outsourced relationship than in an owned one.

The national programme sits behind all of it: 59 logistics zones targeted by 2030 across more than 100 million square metres, with the sector aimed at 10 per cent of gross domestic product. Those zones need tenants, and third-party operators are the tenant class most likely to take space speculatively.

The expo runs from 8 to 10 September at the Riyadh International Convention & Exhibition Center.
